name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q01 - Crystalline versus amorphous two dimensional structures

questiontext.text: Observe the two-dimensional structures of solids X and Y shown below. Identify the correct statement distinguishing solid X from solid Y.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two-dimensional structural representations of solid X and solid Y are provided. Solid X displays a regular, periodically repeating hexagonal pattern, whereas solid Y displays an irregular, disordered network.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A periodically repeating arrangement extending throughout the sample indicates long-range order, while scattered local rings with disordered connections indicate only short-range order.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Crystalline solids possess long-range order, are anisotropic in nature, and melt at a sharp, characteristic temperature. Amorphous solids possess only short-range order, are isotropic in nature, and gradually soften over a range of temperature.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because solid X has a uniform repeating lattice, it is a crystalline solid; hence it is anisotropic and exhibits a sharp melting point. Because solid Y lacks long-range order, it is an amorphous solid; hence its particle arrangement is equivalent in all directions (isotropic), and it softens over a range of temperature.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Comparing the structural features confirms that solid X is anisotropic with a sharp melting point, whereas solid Y is isotropic and softens over a range of temperature.

answer.text: Solid X is anisotropic with a sharp melting point, whereas solid Y is isotropic and softens over a range of temperature.
Solid X is isotropic with a sharp melting point, whereas solid Y is anisotropic and softens over a range of temperature.
Solid X softens over a range of temperature, whereas solid Y melts at a sharp characteristic temperature.
Both solid X and solid Y possess long-range order and are true solids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q02 - Domain alignment in ferrimagnetic solid

questiontext.text: Which type of magnetic behaviour and corresponding example are represented by the schematic alignment of magnetic moments of domains shown below?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows six magnetic domains with arrows indicating the orientation of their magnetic moments: four pointing upwards and two pointing downwards.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Upward arrows represent parallel alignment and downward arrows represent anti-parallel alignment of magnetic moments.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In ferromagnetic substances, all domains align in the same direction. In antiferromagnetic substances, domains align in equal numbers in opposite directions, giving zero net magnetic moment. In ferrimagnetic substances, domains align in parallel and anti-parallel directions in unequal numbers, leaving a small net magnetic moment.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Counting the domains in the diagram gives \(4\) upward (parallel) and \(2\) downward (anti-parallel) moments. Since these opposite orientations are unequal in number, they do not cancel completely, producing a net magnetic moment characteristic of ferrimagnetism. A typical example is magnetite (\(\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{O}_4\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The unequal parallel and anti-parallel alignment confirms ferrimagnetism, as exhibited by \(\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{O}_4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q03 - Anisotropy along different crystal lattice directions

questiontext.text: The diagram below shows a simple two-dimensional pattern of arrangement of two kinds of atoms in a crystal. Why does this crystal exhibit different mechanical properties along directions AB and CD?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A two-dimensional crystal lattice containing two distinct types of atoms (large hollow circles and small filled circles) is shown with two directional lines, AB (vertical) and CD (diagonal).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Mechanical properties such as resistance to shearing stress depend on the types of atoms displaced and the arrangement encountered along the direction of deformation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Anisotropy in crystalline solids arises because the arrangement of constituent particles differs along different directions within the same crystal.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Tracing along the vertical line AB passes only through the row of small filled atoms, whereas tracing along the diagonal line CD passes alternately through both types of atoms (large hollow atoms and small filled atoms). Therefore, deformation along AB displaces rows made of one type of atom, while deformation along CD displaces rows containing two different types of atoms.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because different arrangements of particles are encountered along directions AB and CD, physical and mechanical properties differ along these directions, demonstrating anisotropy.

answer.text: The arrangement along direction AB is amorphous, whereas along direction CD it is crystalline.
Direction AB passes through only one type of atom, whereas direction CD passes through alternating types of atoms, producing different arrangements in different directions.
Both directions have identical particle arrangements, so the crystal is isotropic.
Thermal energy is zero along direction AB and maximum along direction CD.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q04 - Crystal system identification from unit cell parameters

questiontext.text: A unit cell with edge lengths \(a \neq b \neq c\) and axial angles \(\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ\) and \(\beta = 105^\circ\) is illustrated below. Which crystal system and possible Bravais lattice variations correspond to this unit cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The unit cell has unequal edge lengths \(a eq b eq c\) and axial angles \(\alpha = 90^\circ\), \(\gamma = 90^\circ\), and \( eta = 105^\circ eq 90^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In the standard crystallographic convention, \(\alpha\) is the angle between edges \(b\) and \(c\), \( eta\) is between \(a\) and \(c\), and \(\gamma\) is between \(a\) and \(b\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Among the seven crystal systems, the monoclinic system is defined by \(a eq b eq c\) and \(\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ\), \( eta eq 90^\circ\). Its allowed Bravais lattice variations are primitive and end-centred.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Checking the given parameters: all three edges are unequal (\(a eq b eq c\)), two angles are \(90^\circ\) (\(\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ\)), and the third angle \( eta = 105^\circ eq 90^\circ\). This uniquely matches the monoclinic crystal system (for example, monoclinic sulphur or \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)), which has \(2\) Bravais lattices: primitive and end-centred.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Orthorhombic has all angles \(90^\circ\), triclinic has no angle equal to \(90^\circ\), and tetragonal has \(a = b eq c\). Thus, the unit cell belongs to the monoclinic system with primitive and end-centred variations.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q05 - Atomic radius from bcc body diagonal

questiontext.text: In the body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell shown below, the three spheres along the body diagonal touch each other. If the edge length \(a\) of the cube is \(400\text{ pm}\), what is the radius \(r\) of each sphere?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The unit cell is body-centred cubic (bcc) with edge length \(a = 400\text{ pm}\). Three identical spheres of radius \(r\) touch each other along the body diagonal \(c\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The spheres are rigid and touch only along the body diagonal, not along the cube edge or face diagonal.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In a cube of edge length \(a\), the face diagonal is \(b = \sqrt{a^2 + a^2} = \sqrt{2}a\), and the body diagonal is \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{3}a\). Since three spheres touch along the body diagonal, \(c = 4r\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Equating the two expressions for the body diagonal:
\[\sqrt{3}a = 4r\]
\[r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a\]
Substituting \(a = 400\text{ pm}\):
\[r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 400\text{ pm} = 100\sqrt{3}\text{ pm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\), \(r \approx 173.2\text{ pm}\), which is smaller than \(a/2 = 200\text{ pm}\) as expected for a bcc lattice. Therefore, the radius of each sphere is \(100\sqrt{3}\text{ pm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q06 - Two dimensional hexagonal close packing coordination

questiontext.text: In the two-dimensional close-packed layer of identical spheres shown below, what is the coordination number of the central highlighted sphere, and what is the shape of the voids formed within this layer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A two-dimensional close-packed layer of identical spheres is shown in a staggered \(\text{ABAB}\dots\) arrangement, with the centres of the nearest neighbours of a central sphere joined by a red polygon.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coordination number is the number of nearest neighbours in direct contact with a given sphere within the two-dimensional layer.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In two-dimensional hexagonal close packing, each row fits into the depressions of the adjacent row. Joining the centres of the immediate neighbours forms a regular hexagon.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Counting the vertices of the red hexagon surrounding the central highlighted sphere shows that it touches \(6\) neighbouring spheres (\(2\) in its own row, \(2\) in the row above, and \(2\) in the row below). Therefore, the two-dimensional coordination number is \(6\). Between every three mutually touching spheres in this layer, an empty space bounded by three arcs is left, which is triangular in shape (with apex pointing upwards in one row and downwards in the next).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Square close packing has a coordination number of \(4\), whereas this staggered hexagonal close-packed layer has a coordination number of \(6\) and triangular voids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q07 - Schottky defect in ionic crystal lattice

questiontext.text: Identify the point defect illustrated in the ionic crystal lattice below and its effect on the density of the solid.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram depicts a two-dimensional ionic lattice composed of alternating cations (\(+\)) and anions (\(-\)) of comparable sizes, with one cation site and one anion site shown as empty squares (vacancies) and no ions present in interstitial positions.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In an ionic crystal, electrical neutrality requires that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A Schottky defect is a vacancy defect in ionic solids where an equal number of cations and anions are missing from their normal lattice sites. Because mass is removed from the crystal while the overall volume remains nearly constant, density \(d = \frac{m}{V}\) decreases.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Counting the missing ions in the diagram shows \(1\) missing cation and \(1\) missing anion, preserving electrical neutrality. No ion is displaced into an interstitial site, so this is not a Frenkel defect. Since a pair of ions has left the crystal, the mass per unit volume decreases.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The defect shown is a Schottky defect, and it decreases the density of the solid (as seen in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), \(\mathrm{KCl}\), \(\mathrm{CsCl}\), and \(\mathrm{AgBr}\)).

answer.text: Schottky defect; decreases the density of the solid
Frenkel defect; does not change the density of the solid
Interstitial defect; increases the density of the solid
F-centre defect; imparts colour without changing stoichiometry

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q08 - Band theory representation of conductors insulators semiconductors

questiontext.text: The energy band diagrams for three solids I, II, and III are shown below, where shaded regions represent filled valence bands and unshaded regions represent empty conduction bands. Identify I, II, and III correctly.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three band diagrams are shown: I has overlapping filled and empty bands; II has a large forbidden energy gap between the filled valence band and empty conduction band; III has a small energy gap between the filled valence band and empty conduction band.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Electrical conductivity in solids is governed by how easily electrons can move from the filled valence band into the unoccupied conduction band under an applied electric field.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to band theory, overlapping or partially filled bands allow free electron flow (metals/conductors), a large forbidden zone prevents electron excitation (insulators), and a small energy gap allows some electrons to jump to the conduction band, especially as temperature rises (semiconductors).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Matching each diagram: I shows overlapping bands, characteristic of a metal (conductor). II shows a large energy gap, characteristic of an insulator. III shows a small energy gap, characteristic of a semiconductor.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, I is a metal (conductor), II is an insulator, and III is a semiconductor.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q09 - Formula of compound from fcc void occupancy

questiontext.text: In the cubic close-packed (fcc) unit cell shown below, anions \(\mathrm{Y}\) occupy all corners and face centres, while cations \(\mathrm{X}\) occupy the octahedral void at the body centre and only half of the octahedral voids at the edge centres (one such edge-centred void is highlighted). What is the simplest formula of the compound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Anions \(\mathrm{Y}\) form a face-centred cubic (fcc) lattice (occupying all \(8\) corners and \(6\) face centres). Cations \(\mathrm{X}\) occupy the body-centre octahedral void and half of the \(12\) edge-centre octahedral voids.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a cubic unit cell, each corner particle contributes \(\frac{1}{8}\), each face-centre particle contributes \(\frac{1}{2}\), each edge-centre particle contributes \(\frac{1}{4}\), and a body-centre particle contributes \(1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total particles per unit cell \(Z = \sum (\text{number of sites occupied} \times \text{contribution per site})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of \(\mathrm{Y}\) anions per unit cell:
\[N_{\mathrm{Y}} = \left(8 \times \frac{1}{8}\right) + \left(6 \times \frac{1}{2}\right) = 1 + 3 = 4\]
Number of \(\mathrm{X}\) cations per unit cell:
Body-centre contribution \(= 1 \times 1 = 1\).
Edge-centre contribution (for half of the \(12\) edges, i.e., \(6\) edges occupied) \(= 6 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1.5\).
Total \(N_{\mathrm{X}} = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 = \frac{5}{2}\).
Ratio \(\mathrm{X} : \mathrm{Y} = \frac{5}{2} : 4 = 5 : 8\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying by \(2\) gives whole-number stoichiometry \(\mathrm{X}_5\mathrm{Y}_8\). The ratio \(2.5/4 = 0.625 = 5/8\) is exact. Thus, the simplest formula of the compound is \(\mathrm{X}_5\mathrm{Y}_8\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q10 - Type of semiconductor from doped silicon lattice

questiontext.text: The schematic diagram below represents a silicon crystal doped with a trace amount of an element E, creating a positive hole (electron vacancy) at one of the covalent bonds. Which element could E be, and what type of semiconductor is formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a silicon crystal (group \(14\), four valence electrons per atom) in which one lattice site is occupied by an impurity atom E. Three of the bonds around E have complete electron pairs, while the fourth bond has only one electron and a missing electron (a positive hole).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Silicon requires four valence electrons per atom to form four complete covalent bonds with its four nearest neighbours.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Doping a group \(14\) element (\(\mathrm{Si}\) or \(\mathrm{Ge}\)) with an electron-deficient group \(13\) element (\(\mathrm{B}\), \(\mathrm{Al}\), or \(\mathrm{Ga}\)) having \(3\) valence electrons leaves one covalent bond incomplete, creating an electron vacancy called an electron hole (positive hole), which produces a \(p\)-type semiconductor.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because atom E forms three complete covalent bonds and leaves one electron missing in the fourth bond, E must have \(3\) valence electrons (group \(13\)). Among the choices, boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) is a group \(13\) element, whereas phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) and arsenic (\(\mathrm{As}\)) belong to group \(15\) (producing \(n\)-type semiconductors with an extra mobile electron) and germanium (\(\mathrm{Ge}\)) belongs to group \(14\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Under an electric field, electrons move through these holes toward the positive plate, making it appear as if positively charged holes move toward the negative plate. Thus, E is boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) and the crystal is a \(p\)-type semiconductor.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q11 - Cation vacancy concentration in doped NaCl

questiontext.text: The crystal defect shown below occurs when molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is doped with \(10^{-3}\text{ mol}\%\) of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\). How many cation vacancies are present per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is doped with \(10^{-3}\text{ mol}\%\) of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\). The diagram illustrates one \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion substituting for \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) and leaving one cation site vacant.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Avogadro constant \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\). Doping \(10^{-3}\text{ mol}\%\) means \(10^{-3}\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\) is present per \(100\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
To maintain electrical neutrality, each \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion replaces two \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) ions, occupying one site and creating \(1\) cation vacancy. Thus, the number of cation vacancies equals the number of \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ions introduced.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Moles of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\) per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\):
\[n_{\mathrm{SrCl}_2} = \frac{10^{-3}}{100} = 10^{-5}\text{ mol}\]
Number of \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ions per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\):
\[N_{\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}} = 10^{-5}\text{ mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 6.022 \times 10^{18}\]
Since each \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion creates \(1\) cation vacancy, the number of cation vacancies per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is \(6.022 \times 10^{18}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the exponent: \(10^{-3}\text{ mol}\% = 10^{-5}\text{ mol}\) per mole of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), and \(10^{-5} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{18}\). Therefore, the concentration of cation vacancies is \(6.022 \times 10^{18}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
